clue.text: Webster has the odds-I back red

parts.note: SP is the starting price, the odds offered on a horse at the off

indicators.note: back tells us the colour word is written in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone at the roulette wheel, odds in mind, puts a stake on red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Webster' looks like a surname (the dictionary maker or dramatist), but it is one who weaves webs. 'back' turns RED into DER.
explanation.definitionFit: A webster is literally a weaver of webs, and the spinner of webs in nature is this eight-legged creature.

clue.text: Section of page one, EEC Constitution

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: a constitution is a make-up or composition, so these three letters are made up afresh

explanation.surface: Part of the front page is given over to a story on the European Economic Community's constitution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitution' rearranges EEC into ECE. The EEC was the European Economic Community, forerunner of the EU.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece is a portion or part of something, just as a section is.

clue.text: Tip off? Yes, hard point is broken

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters of these two words are reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone confirms that a hard point has snapped off the end of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yes' is a link that answers the question 'Tip off?'. 'is broken' rearranges HARDPOINT.
explanation.definitionFit: To tip someone off is to give them a quiet warning or suggestion, a gentle hint.

clue.text: General opinion, perhaps true, about record

indicators.note: about places the shuffled word around the record
perhaps suggests a possible version of the word true, its letters rearranged

parts.note: EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A view held by most people, possibly accurate, concerning someone's track record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' turns TRUE into RUTE, and 'about' puts it around EP: R-EP-UTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Repute is reputation, the standing someone has in the common estimation of others.

clue.text: Sick and tired, utterly, of this kind of youth

parts.note: ill means sick
spent means completely exhausted

explanation.surface: A jaded figure looks back, sick and utterly worn out, on a misused adolescence.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the familiar phrase about a youth wasted in idle or dissolute living.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock phrase describes a youth squandered in wasteful or dissolute ways.

clue.text: Book pub, with no money, on a minor highway

parts.note: an inn is a pub
O is nought, nothing
cents are units of money
taken as written
a B-road is a minor road in Britain, below an A-road

explanation.surface: A traveller books a stay at an inn, though penniless, on a country road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb (reserve the pub) but names Mark Twain's travel book. A B-road is a British secondary road.
explanation.definitionFit: The Innocents Abroad is Mark Twain's 1869 travel book about Americans touring Europe and the Holy Land.

clue.text: Jewel held by mysterious alien subject

indicators.note: held by places the jewel inside the shuffled word
mysterious suggests the word alien is muddled into an unclear order

parts.note: a gem is a jewel

explanation.surface: A precious stone is in the possession of a strange extraterrestrial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mysterious' rearranges ALIEN to LIEAN, and 'held by' puts GEM inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: In feudal times a liegeman was a vassal owing allegiance to a lord: a subject.

clue.text: Peter's small contribution to Rome

parts.note: Peter's ... was the annual penny tax paid to the papacy in Rome; small coins make the contribution

explanation.surface: Saint Peter makes a modest donation to the Church in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter's pence was a medieval levy paid to the Pope, still the name for donations to the Holy See.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter's pence is the traditional name for offerings sent to the Holy See, made in small coins.

clue.text: Mythical sufferer from Malvolio's sickness

parts.note: in Twelfth Night Olivia tells Malvolio he is sick of self-love; the Greek youth who loved his own reflection had the same ailment

explanation.surface: A figure from legend suffers from the same malady as Shakespeare's steward.
explanation.walkthrough: Malvolio, the puritanical steward in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, is told 'you are sick of self-love'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek youth fell in love with his own reflection, the archetype of vanity and self-love.

clue.text: Back-payment concerning firm member seen in trouble

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Co is short for company, a firm
MP is a Member of Parliament

indicators.note: in trouble describes the word seen as disturbed, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Arrears of pay concern a company's partner who has been spotted in difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' rearranges SEEN to ENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Recompense is compensation paid back for loss or service, a repayment.

clue.text: Standard article from a girl

indicators.note: from signals taking the article away from the name

parts.note: Norma is a girl's name
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A typical piece of writing produced by a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article from' means remove the article A from NORMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is a standard or usual pattern against which things are measured.

clue.text: Can Times make changes of significance in words ?

indicators.note: make changes asks for the letters of the two words to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A question whether this newspaper can alter what words mean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make changes' rearranges CANTIMES. The surface knowingly mentions the paper itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Semantics is the study of meaning, so the adjective describes the meaning carried by words.

clue.text: She advised a long time without anger, looking back

indicators.note: looking back means the assembled letters are read in the opposite direction
without in its old sense of outside, so the long time goes around the anger

parts.note: an age is a long time
ire is anger

explanation.surface: A woman gave counsel for ages, free of rage, reflecting on the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside: A-IRE-GE, and 'looking back' turns that into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman legend the nymph counselled King Numa, so her name now means a female adviser.

clue.text: First item knocked down to Pierre

parts.note: an item knocked down at auction is a lot
I is the Roman numeral one, first

explanation.surface: The opening item at an auction is sold to a Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: Lot one, the first item at auction, becomes LOT I. Pierre Loti was a French novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre Loti was the pen name of the French naval officer and novelist Julien Viaud.

clue.text: Shades of meaning of public individuals

parts.note: overt means open, public
ones are individual persons

explanation.surface: Subtle meanings conveyed by figures in public life.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtones are subtle additional implications or suggestions beyond the literal sense.

clue.text: Neighbourhood girl almost makes a hit

parts.note: near means close by, in the neighbourhood
miss is a girl

explanation.surface: A local girl very nearly becomes a success.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the phrase 'almost makes a hit'; the noun names such a close shave.
explanation.definitionFit: A near miss is a shot or attempt that narrowly fails to strike its target.

clue.text: Alleviated nasty time at dig

indicators.note: nasty suggests the words are treated roughly, their letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Relief came after an unpleasant spell at an archaeological excavation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' rearranges TIMEATDIG.
explanation.definitionFit: To mitigate is to lessen the severity of something, to ease or relieve it.

clue.text: A bit of crafty graft, taking chaps in

indicators.note: taking chaps in means the jumbled word holds the men inside it
crafty suggests the word graft is cunningly rearranged

parts.note: chaps are men

explanation.surface: A small piece of cunning corruption involves bringing men on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crafty' rearranges GRAFT to FRAGT, and 'taking ... in' puts MEN inside: FRAG-MEN-T.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragment is a small broken-off part of something.

clue.text: Causes upset by outburst

parts.note: per means by, as in per post

indicators.note: out signals the following word is put out of order

explanation.surface: Someone throws others into disarray with a sudden fit of temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outburst' splits into 'out' and 'burst': 'out' rearranges BURST to TURBS.
explanation.definitionFit: To perturb is to unsettle or disturb someone, upsetting them.

clue.text: Cowper's poetical work

definitions.meaning: William Cowper's long blank-verse poem of 1785
a piece of work to be done, a job

explanation.surface: A reference to the verse of the eighteenth-century poet William Cowper.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem by Cowper bears this title; separately, the word means a job or duty assigned.

clue.text: For good French it's elementary

parts.note: car is French for because, for
bon is French for good

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that the French word for good is simple stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' applies to both words: CAR is French 'for' and BON French 'good'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbon is a chemical element, so it is something elementary.

clue.text: Where war prisoners show the way to a convict

parts.note: St is short for street, a way
lag, as in old lag, is slang for a convict

explanation.surface: Captured soldiers guide a jailbird out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show' is a link: the rest shows how the word is built. A stalag was a German prisoner-of-war camp.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalag was a German camp for captured soldiers in the Second World War.

clue.text: Trustworthy old regiment

definitions.meaning: the ... Regiment (North Lancashire) was a British Army infantry regiment until 1970

explanation.surface: A dependable military unit of long standing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means faithful and dependable; it was also the name of a former Lancashire infantry regiment.

clue.text: Bring round a horse with big talk

indicators.note: round means the first word goes around the other pieces

parts.note: gee-gee, GG, is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to lead a horse round, talking grandly as they do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring' is not an instruction but the word that goes 'round' A GG: BR-AGG-ING.
explanation.definitionFit: Bragging is boastful speech, talking oneself up.

clue.text: No centre-half unfortunately for this occasion

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests those letters suffer a mishap and are jumbled
half here takes the first half of the word centre

explanation.surface: A football team without its central defender is unlucky this time.
explanation.walkthrough: A centre-half is a central defender in football. 'half' takes CEN from 'centre', and 'unfortunately' rearranges it to NCE.
explanation.definitionFit: For the nonce is an old phrase meaning for the present occasion only.

clue.text: Unique way A Tale of Two Cities was dramatized

definitions.meaning: single, sole, the one of its kind

definitions.text: way A Tale of Two Cities was dramatized
definitions.meaning: The 1899 stage adaptation of Dickens's novel

explanation.surface: A one-off approach to putting Dickens's novel on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means sole or unique; with way after it, it gives the title of the famous stage version of Dickens's novel.

clue.text: Executor put the bite on worker-—that's too much !

parts.note: exor is a legal abbreviation for executor
bit is the past tense of bite, having put teeth in
the worker ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: An estate's administrator squeezed a labourer for money, which was excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put the bite on' is slang for demanding money, but here it is simply BIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Exorbitant means excessive, far beyond what is reasonable, especially of prices.

clue.text: Set apart, I do least damage

indicators.note: damage tells us these words are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone separated from others claims to cause the smallest harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damage' rearranges IDOLEAST.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolated means separated from others, kept alone.

clue.text: No theologian, journalist made a Homeric slip

parts.note: DD is Doctor of Divinity, a theologian
ed, an editor, is the crossword's usual journalist

explanation.surface: A journalist with no religious learning committed a blunder worthy of the Greek poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to Horace's saying that even good Homer nods, makes a lapse.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace said even great Homer sometimes dozes off, so to make such a lapse is to doze off like him.
